I. Rationale 
A. The Economic Context and Development challenges 
Guyana is an open, predominantly agricultural economy with considerable natural resources. For more 
than two decades following its independence in 1966, Guyana operated a State-controlled economic 
system with major productive sectors (sugar, rice, bauxite, and gold) and financial institutions all brought 
under direct government control. Prices were extensively controlled, foreign exchange was rationed, and 
government-owned consumer and marketing agencies were established. As a result, private sector growth 
languished, a parallel economy emerged, and government administration became overburdened. 
In addition, the economy experienced a steady decline in output and large macroeconomic imbalances. 
Real gross domestic product (GDP) fell at an average rate of 3 percent per annum during the 1980’s. 
Inadequate policy responses led to a sharp deterioration in Guyana’s external terms of trade and weak 
external demand for its major exports led to lower production, large fiscal deficits, high inflation, depletion of 
gross external reserves, and a sharp rise in external indebtedness. By 1988 external debt arrears had 
accumulated to about US$500 million or 315 percent of GDP. 
In mid-1988, the Government adopted a medium-term Economic Recovery Programme (ERP) with the 
support of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other donors, which aimed at fundamentally shifting 
the economy toward a market-oriented system. As part of the ERP and the economic programmes agreed 
with the IMF, the Government implemented economic and structural policies that, by 1991, led to a turn 
around in economic performance. Following sizeable declines in 1989-90, real GDP grew by over 5 
percent in 1992-99; inflation declined markedly, from over 100 percent to single digits; the fiscal and 
external deficits were reduced substantially; and private capital inflows rose significantly. Guyana made 
substantial progress in implementing economic reforms that focused on privatization of public entities, 
enhancing private sector participation, strengthening the financial and regulatory frameworks, improving 
access to basic health and education, and increasing social sector spending. 
In May 1999 the IMF and World Bank determined that Guyana had satisfied all the conditions for 
reaching the completion point under the original Highly Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative. Under 
this initiative, the debt relief to Guyana from the international community amounts to US$256 million in net 
present value (NPV) terms or about US$440 million in nominal terms. In addition, the IMF and the World 
Bank agreed in November 2000, to support a comprehensive debt reduction package for Guyana under the 
enhanced HIPC Initiative. This debt relief package will save Guyana about $329 million in NPV terms or 
about $590 million in nominal terms. 
Notwithstanding these improvements, the Guyanese economy still faces considerable difficulties including 
adverse external terms of trade shocks, adverse weather conditions and political uncertainty. The main 
economic challenges are to raise real growth rates, which have averaged just over ½ percent since 1997; 
expand the production base; and improve the economic infrastructure. 
The urgent reduction of widespread income and human poverty represents a major challenge for the 
Government and people of Guyana. The 1999 Guyana Social and Living Conditions survey (GSLC)
suggests that (based on the head-count measure of the incidence of poverty) 36 percent of the population 2
live in absolute poverty and 19 percent in critical poverty.1 Poverty in Guyana is heavily concentrated in 
the hinterland and rural coastal areas. Income poverty can be mainly attributed to inadequate and uneven 
economic growth and insufficient emphasis on rights-based development, which leads to inequities in 
access to economic resources and social services. 
There is growing unemployment and underemployment, which extends to the educated. Poverty tends to 
be community based and many of the poor work in agriculture without adequate access to land, finances, 
and facilities. Amerindian communities are among the poorest in Guyana. But the poor are also to be 
found among the rural population and those who eke out a living in the informal sector. Guyana's 
pandemic poverty is also reflected in knowledge and communication deprivation, unhealthy 
lifestyles, the inability to exercise civil and political rights, the erosion of dignity and self-respect, 
and environmental impoverishment. 
Guyana has made significant progress in promoting human development. However, challenges remain. 
Health indicators are still inferior to those of sister CARICOM states. Some 44 percent of households are 
living in congested circumstances, about 36 percent of the population have no electricity and no access to 
piped water, and roughly 84 percent of the population live with one or more basic needs unmet. HIV/AIDS 
in Guyana has spread beyond commercial sex workers (CSWs) and their clients and intravenous drug 
users. Its prevalence has increased among other groups in the society. Gender disparities, regional 
inequities, and customary patterns of discrimination (for example, against children) still persist. Social 
problems can also be traced to weaknesses in governance: insufficient participation, an inefficient judiciary, 
corrupt administrative practices, and insufficient accountability. 
Politically, with the People's Progressive Party (PPP)/Civic victory at the polls in 1992, there was a sense 
among the populace that Guyana had truly joined the international community of multi-party democracies. 
This raised the expectations of civil society, especially in respect of quality of life and wider participation, 
and created a more fluid and unstable environment. The general elections of 1997 ended in controversy 
with the main opposition party challenging the results and refusing to recognise the Government. To 
defuse the tensions that ensued, the PPP/Civic Government agreed to limit its term in office to 3 rather than 
the Constitutionally stipulated 5 years, and all parties agreed to the initiation of a process of constitutional 
reform. The recommendations coming out of the broad-based consultations with people of every stratum of 
the society have been compiled by a Parliamentary Committee and are being addressed by Parliament. 
The challenge that now faces the Government, if it is to deliver on peoples' high expectations, is to promote 
good governance, ensure sustained growth, and embrace broad-based, pro-poor, rights-oriented 
development. The political and economic situation in the country was complicated during 2000 by the 
deterioration in Guyana's relations with two of its contiguous neighbours. Venezuela’s claim to 60.5 
percent (130,000 sq. km.) of Guyana’s territory west of the Essequibo River resurfaced, as did the territorial 
dispute with Suriname. To date, neither border problem has affected diplomatic and trade-links between 
Guyana and the respective countries. 
B. National Priorities 
Guyana's current Constitution, promulgated in 1980, promises the basic human rights to every citizen of 
Guyana and directs the State to protect those rights by establishing a just system in all aspects of national 
 
1 This represented a significant reduction from the 1992/93 period when the HIES/LSMS found the rates to be 43 and 28 percent, respectively. 
However, this improvement notwithstanding, Guyana performance remains well below that of other Caribbean countries. 3
life, including social, economic and political life, and protecting the lives, property and liberty of the people. 
It sets objectives that emphasize equity and recognizes the importance of participation. Further, the 
emphasis on human rights has been the thrust of the work of the Constitution Reform Commission (CRC) 
during 2000. However, there is need for appropriately fashioned legislation that gives citizens the right to 
have their basic human rights protected in law. 
Guyana is committed to development that is non-discriminatory, participatory and broadly shared. 
Government endorses development that secures the rights of all men, women and children; improves 
health, education, and the general standard of living; promotes better governance; and removes patterns of 
inequality, disparity and discrimination. Consistent with this endorsement, Guyana has ratified most of the 
international conventions dealing with human rights, the rights of women and children, the treatment of 
labour, and the environment. It is significant that Guyana has ratified the International Covenants on 
Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights 
(ICCPR), the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICEAFRD), the Convention on the 
Elimination of all forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), and the Convention on the Rights of 
the Child (CoRC) 
The Government is well aware of the critical nature of development challenges facing the country and has, 
over the past decade, embarked on ambitious initiatives to overcome poverty with the assistance of the 
international donor community. At the same time, numerous targeted programmes have been combined 
with social mobilization to provide special assistance to the extremely poor. More recently, Government 
has used the draft National Development Strategy (NDS), a document produced by Civil Society, to 
develop its Interim Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (I-PRSP). The I-PRSP articulates Government's 
poverty reduction goals as (i) creating opportunities for income generation; (ii) job creation; (iii) reducing 
mortality rates, (iv) achieving universal primary education; and (v) eliminating gender disparity in education. 
These goals are broadly consistent with international development goals. Their attainment is predicated on 
(i) high and sustainable growth rates; (ii) improvement in social conditions; and (iii) addressing uneven 
spatial distribution of population. To realize these goals, government proposes to adopt a five-pronged 
strategy that comprises: (i) maintaining a sound macroeconomic, trade and investment framework; (ii) 
improving the business environment; (iii) improving social services (including health, education, nutrition, 
family planning, and access to safe water and housing); (iv) maintaining and expanding economic 
infrastructure; and (v) implementing poverty reduction programmes consistent with the thrust of the I-PRSP. 
The I-PRSP emphasizes the importance of stakeholder participation for poverty reduction and makes 
participation of key stakeholders a central component of the programme of action. This action plan 
underscores the role of the State as facilitator and details Government's strategy for improving (I) 
macroeconomic and fiscal structure, (ii) diversifying growth, (iii) supporting private sector development, (iv) 
reorienting public expenditures, (v) reforming the financial sector, (vi) institutionalizing decentralization, (vii) 
ensuring good governance, (viii) reforming the Civil Service, (ix) improving aid effectiveness, and (x) 
strengthening the role of Civil Society. Recognizing the importance of improved coordination and efficient 
implementation, the I-PRSP proposes the establishment of a Poverty Reduction Strategy Coordination and 
Implementation Unit (PRSCIU) that will work in close collaboration with both Civil Society and the Donor 
Community. The strategy builds on the significant progress achieved over the last decade in policy 
reforms, especially in the areas of economic liberalization, governance and better resource allocation. 4
The public sector budgetary allocations proposed in the I-PRSP will focus primarily on health, education, 
housing, and economic infrastructure. Already, the MFIs like the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), 
Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), and the World Bank have funded programmes that will contribute to 
a realization of the I-PRSP goals. 
C. UN System Priorities 
Currently, only four UN agencies have resident offices in Guyana and work within the Resident Coordinator 
System: (i) The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), (ii) The United Nations Fund for 
Children (UNICEF), (iii) The Pan-American Health Organization/World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO), 
and (iv) The IMF. By the first quarter of 2001 the World Bank is expected to establish a presence as well. 
However, Guyana also receives invaluable assistance from other UN agencies such as FAO, ILO, ITU, 
UNECLAC, UNESCO, UNFPA, UNICEF, UNIDO, WFP, (had office until August 2000) WIPO and WTO. 
Guyana also receives assistance from bilateral donors, as well as from the IADB, the CDB, and the 
European Union (EU). 
The thrust of UN system assistance has so far been in the following strategic areas: 
 Joint advocacy and policy advice on the implementation of conventions, declarations and 
programmes of action of global conferences 
 Capacity-building and institutional strengthening of key entities 
 Support to decentralization and participation; 
 Strengthening of data collection, dissemination and participatory monitoring. 
With the establishment of the Resident Coordinator System the UNCT in Guyana has put in place 
institutional mechanisms to enhance inter-agency collaboration, such as regular Heads of Agencies 
meetings and Inter-Agency Thematic Groups (IATGs). A major product of this development has been the 
completion of the Common Country Assessment (CCA) in 2000. The process and the analytical work that 
culminated in the CCA document enabled the individual UN system agencies to arrive at a shared 
understanding of the development challenges facing Guyana. It allowed also for a re-commitment of each 
agency to contribute to the UN Country Team's focus on key priority areas in which the UN system has an 
obvious and distinct comparative advantage. 
This document--the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF)--is based on the 
analytical work and findings of the CCA and is aimed at achieving a greater impact of UN System 
cooperation through the preparation of a complementary set of programmes and projects under an 
umbrella document. The idea of an UNDAF dates back to July 1997 when it was introduced by the UN 
Secretary General (and embraced and endorsed by the General Assembly) as the centerpiece of United 
Nations development cooperation at the country level. The UNDAF serves as a planning framework for all 
UN development funds, programmes and agencies and reflects common areas of programme action in 
response to national development priorities and needs. As explained by the UN Secretary General in his 
report on UN reform, 
“In order to achieve goal oriented collaboration, coherence and mutual reinforcement, the 
United Nations programmes of assistance will be formulated and presented as part of a 5
single United Nations Development Assistance Framework with common objectives and 
time-frame.” 
Thus, the next harmonized programme cycle of UN agencies in Guyana (2001-2005) will coincide with the 
UNDAF timeframe and commence with a coherent set of UN-supported interventions. The UNDAF builds 
upon Guyana's endorsement of human rights and is based on the provisions of the current Constitution 
(and the proposed constitutional changes) and numerous international human rights instruments to which 
Guyana is a signatory. The UNDAF seeks specifically to provide a framework for UN System cooperation 
with the Government and people of Guyana to ensure the realization by all people of their economic, social, 
cultural, civil and political rights. It is organized principally around the individual rights enshrined in ICESCR 
and the ICCPR but it also takes cognizance of those rights enshrined in all International Conventions and 
the Programmes of Action of the World Conferences. 
The UNCT believes that adoption of a rights-based (as opposed to a needs-based) approach to 
development will enable better support to Government's agenda for poverty reduction for at least the 
following reasons: 
 According the highest priority to the most deprived brings UN system assistance in line with the 
national poverty reduction strategy (since the poor tends to be most deprived of their rights); 
 Systematic attention to governance (i.e. issues of discrimination, participation and accountability) 
enables the UN system to address the basic underlying causes of poverty and enhances the 
impact of UN System assistance; 
 Using the international covenants on economic, social, cultural, civil and political rights as the 
reference framework provides a comprehensive development framework, a basis for a coordinated 
follow-up to UN conferences, and supports implementation of conventions and declarations. 
The UNCT in Guyana has aligned itself behind the national government’s strategic plan to reduce poverty 
and promote sustainable human development. For almost four decades, various UN projects and 
programmes have directed assistance aimed at achieving an eclectic mix of social and economic goals in a 
collaborative and synergistic process. Through this experience the UNCT now has a position of trust in its 
partnership with the government and people of Guyana. Over the years, the UNCT has implemented 
numerous project interventions. Equally important, it has brought examples of best practice from other 
countries that have created myriad opportunities for experiential learning and capacity building. 
Based on its past experience in Guyana, its neutrality, and the Government trust that it enjoys, the UNCT 
has a strong comparative advantage in the area of work in support of poverty reduction. For this reason, 
the UNCT in Guyana is best placed to support Government's poverty reduction agenda in the following 
related areas: 
 Macro-level interventions:- By supporting pursuit of a sustainable, pro-poor growth path, through 
continued support to the restructuring of budgets in line with the 20/20 initiative and the formulation 
of policies to counter the negative effects of globalization. 
 Interventions that reach the poor:- By supporting government in the delivery of basic goods and 
services to the poor in an effective, efficient and accountable way, by way of (I) capacity-building 6
initiatives at all levels, and (ii) generating awareness of economic, social, cultural, civil and political 
rights among the poor. 
 Monitoring and Evaluation Interventions:- By assisting the government in the design of custommade interventions that target the most deprived through dis-aggregated monitoring and evaluation 
systems, the implementation of pilot projects (for people to gain better control over resources), and 
concentrated assistance in areas of greatest deprivation. 
II. Goals of Assistance 
In support of Government's long-term development objective to "reduce poverty to very low and tolerable 
levels," and in line with the goals set at the WSSD (to reduce the incidence of extreme poverty by one half 
by 2015), UN system assistance will have as its long-term goal the reduction in human poverty and the 
elimination of absolute income poverty by 2015. 
The UN System assistance will seek to address the root causes of poverty. As such, it will be guided by a 
human rights based approach to development and will emphasize the development of partnerships in order 
to bring about the following long-term development outcomes: 
(i) Progressive realization by the Guyanese people (beginning with those most deprived) of 
their economic, social, cultural, civil, and political rights. 
One of the main reasons for poverty in Guyana is the existence of various forms of 
discrimination and inequality. It is therefore, imperative to address the plight of those who 
are most disadvantaged and whose rights are most denied. This will require rights-based 
analyses that expose the greatest areas of poverty and discrimination. It will require also 
expanding the enabling legal framework and protective mechanisms. Since development 
resources in Guyana will continue to be scarce over the foreseeable future, every attention 
will have to be given to issues of phasing and targeting. 
(ii) Facilitating meaningful participation of all Guyanese in the development process. 
The UN System approach considers participation to be the right of citizens and every 
community, the denial of which limits their ability to own and control the development 
process and compromises its sustainability. Government has also subscribed to this view 
in its I-PRSP by emphasizing the importance of social mobilization, decentralization, and 
the integral involvement of all stakeholders (including the private sector) in the 
development process. A central task of the UNDAF will be the systematic identification and 
removal of impediments to meaningful participation. 
(iii) Assisting the State to respect, protect, and fulfil the rights of all citizens and to be 
accountable for the positive and negative responsibilities associated with this duty. 
This outcome commits UN Agencies to the propagation of rights awareness to both the 
State and the populace. Advocacy and other interventions will aim at encouraging the 
State to place accountability at the centre of development. The State will be encouraged 
and assisted to (a) establish the appropriate legislative and administrative mechanisms for 7
ensuring respect for rights; (b) ensure that neither State nor non-State entities and actors 
deny citizens their rights; and (c) approach resource allocation and prioritization in a 
manner that is conducive to the fulfillment of rights. 8
III. Objectives of Assistance and Cooperation Strategies 
The UNDAF approach is to identify, under every cluster of rights, cooperation strategies that facilitate the 
progressive realization of human rights and sustainable human development. The pursuit of this objective 
will be through sets of interventions that can be broadly categorized as follows: 
 The formulation of policies that create an enabling environment (including especially collection and 
dissemination of relevant data and research and the strengthening of the body of laws and the 
legal framework); 
 The implementation of pilot and demonstration projects and programmes and replication of 
innovative projects; 
 Support to decentralisation, meaningful participation, and accountability at the local level. 
A. Right to adequate standard of living 
 
The inability of some 35 percent of Guyanese households to secure adequate food, clothing, shelter, safe 
drinking water and sanitation, and a safe environment (a right covered under Art. 11 of the ICESCR) is a 
manifestation of the depth of human and income poverty in Guyana. The UNCT is well positioned to 
contribute to the progressive realization of the right to an adequate standard of living in Guyana. The UN 
agencies will continue to build on past programmes and projects that contributed to improving the standard 
of living and will support the I-PRSP strategy of refocusing public expenditures to facilitate improvements in 
the areas of health, water and sanitation, housing, and safety nets. These actions are consistent with what 
Government agreed to at various international Summits. 
In contributing to Government's efforts to ensure these rights, the UN system agencies' objective will be to 
increase access to adequate, safe and healthy food, housing, drinking water and sanitation by fostering an 
enabling environment, preventing natural and human-made disasters, and improving the targeting of the 
most vulnerable populations. Essentially, the strategy to be adopted by the UN System agencies will entail: 
 Progressive elimination of policy, legislative, and institutional constraints that prevent communities 
and individuals from enjoying the right to an adequate standard of living; 
 Better targeting of the most deprived with a view to building and enhancing capacity so that they 
become self-reliant and empowered; 
 Support for the prevention and mitigation of natural and human-made disasters that directly affect 
the standard of living of the poorest. 
More specifically, the UNCT will: 
(i) Support policy and law formulation/amendments that have a direct impact on the 
standard of living and the environment. 
In order to ensure equal access of all to land and housing, the UN system will jointly support the review and 
amendment of existing discriminatory laws/regulations regarding land and property rights, as well as the 
development of land reform policy. Guyana has signed and/or ratified several international conventions 
relating to environmental wellbeing. The UN System agencies will continue to support the amendment, 9
enactment and, where necessary, drafting of new laws and standards regarding food safety, housing, and 
environmental wellbeing, and will work with Government and stakeholders generally to facilitate the 
implementation of these conventions to the fullest extent. Current bilateral donor interventions directed at 
the Lands and Surveys Department and UNDP interventions aimed at exploring opportunities for breaking 
the logjam on the creation of National Protected Areas in Guyana fall within the ambit of the activities 
referred to here. 
At least over the short-term, globalization and Government’s liberalization policies may impact negatively 
on purchasing power and income distribution, and consequently on food security and poverty reduction. In 
recognition of this reality, the UN System Agencies will seek to provide advisory services and support for 
policy-makers that, among other things facilitate analyses and the design of strategies to counter these 
potential negative effects and contribute to the elimination of indirect factors that contribute to hunger and 
poor nutritional status, address easier access to credit, improve the delivery of extension services, and 
improve marketing intelligence and marketing strategies. For example, already there is a project request 
(No. 0-XI-Guy-053) worth some US$306,207 that addresses "Strengthening Food Control Capacity and the 
National Codex Control Point of the Government of Guyana to facilitate International Trade and Commerce" 
that has been submitted to FAO Technical Cooperation Programme for financial consideration. 
(ii) Initiate and replicate innovative projects and programmes in order to increase 
access to sufficient and nutritious food for the most deprived. 
Given Guyana’s large landmass, the gradual opening up of remote areas is important to enable farmers to 
realize their potential. The UN system agencies will initiate and support efforts aimed at improving physical 
access to new lands and the provision of basic services that aid the expansion and diversification of income 
earning opportunities. Emphasis will be placed on support for "Food for Work" schemes that mitigate the 
effects of food insecurity and programmes that address micronutrient deficiencies, particularly in the remote 
communities. Continued attention will be given to the promotion of improved feeding practices (breastfeeding for babies and the feeding of young children), the provision of fortified food commodities via 
selected programmes that combine nutrition education and training. 
Recognizing that the Amerindian communities in the hinterland are especially vulnerable continued support 
will be given to the promotion of eco-tourism, community forestry, and sustainable livelihoods as ways of 
ensuring access of the most deprived to appropriate and sustainable standards of living. Attention will also 
be given to the promotion of access to suitable technologies for sustainability and stability, with emphasis 
on conservation of soil and other natural resources, integrated pest management, and post-harvest 
operations. 
Additionally, through the Telefood Special Fund, the FAO can direct resources to the tune of US$10,000 
per project (or US$30,000 annually) in support of community-based projects that are entrepreneurial and 
related to food production activities. 
(iii) Assist government and decentralized bodies to better target the most deprived. 
Recognizing that landless and near landless households are usually prone to violation of their rights to food 
and housing, the WFS recommended the development and periodical update of a national Food Insecurity 
and Vulnerability Information and Mapping System (FIVIMS) to inform targeted programmes that enhance 10
the entitlements of these groups.2 Relying especially on the expertise of UNDP, UNICEF, FAO, and WFP 
in this area, the UN System agencies will assist decentralized authorities in identifying and targeting these 
groups in the population with a view to formulating and implementing appropriate intervention strategies. 
The FIVIMS will be people-centred and participatory. 
The FAO is especially capable of assisting the Government with the adaptation of the FIVIM methodology 
and while there has been no official request for assistance with the establishment of FIVIMS, Guyana's 
request for assistance in the strengthening of agricultural information systems and the conduct of an 
agricultural census has been submitted to UNDP Guyana for financial consideration. 
Recognizing the importance of transferring skills and competencies to the decentralized authorities, the UN 
System agencies will also expand and intensify initiatives aimed at improving the technical and managerial 
capacity of these institutions with a view to enhancing accountability, transparency, and efficiency in the 
provisioning of the goods and services required for removing the barriers to food security. 
(iv) Support prevention and mitigation of natural and human-made disasters. 
Guyana is not prone to natural disasters. However, floods frequently affect coastal regions, and climatic 
phenomena like El Niño and La Niña can have a devastating impact on agricultural producers generally, 
and hinterland communities in particular. If the detrimental impact of natural disasters is to be limited, it is 
necessary that disaster prevention and mitigation measures be in place both to protect productive assets 
and to provide emergency interventions. Building on its experience in the mitigation of natural disasters, 
the UN System agencies will provide support to prevention policies and activities and aid in building 
capacity to anticipate and to deal with emergencies. For example, the UNCT could explore possibilities for 
the utilization of technologies such as those available through the CTBTO that aid in the prediction of 
climatic phenomena. 
B. Right to Protection and Assistance to the Family, Women and Children 
The UN System agencies are keen to contribute to Government’s pursuit and eventual realization of its 
commitments under the ICESCR, the CEDAW, the CRC, and other international conventions that deal with 
rights to protection and assistance to the family, reproduction rights, right to special protection and 
assistance to children and young persons, right to protection of women and children against any form of 
violence, abuse and exploitation, and the right to social security. The UN System agencies in Guyana have 
a comparative advantage and a long history of working with women and children and promoting gender 
equality. 
Using its vast experience in social mobilization, the UNCT intends to cooperate at the macro, community, 
and programme levels to realize the following objectives, all of which are in line with the conventions 
referred to above as well as the goals of the Beijing Platform for Action and of the ICPD: 
 To promote gender equality and to support special protection and assistance measures for women 
of reproductive age and children, through (a) social mobilization and rights-awareness, (b)

promotion of participation, and (c) joint follow-up of relevant global conferences, conventions and

 To eliminate the worst forms of violence, abuse, and exploitation of women and children through 
the combined use of advocacy, prevention and rehabilitation. 
 To support the design and development of social safety nets, especially for the elderly, the

More specifically, the UNCT will: 
(i) Assist Government to close the gap between international and national laws and 
between policy and implementation in relation to the implementation of international 
conventions such as CEDAW and CRC and the social development commitments 
arising out of the ICPD and the Beijing Platform for Action. 
The UNCT will continue to advocate the priorities of these conventions on behalf of the vulnerable. 
Consistent with the 20/20 pact, the UNCT will continue to advocate also the need to ensure that the 
maximum possible budgetary allocations of available resources are made available for implementing 
economic, social, and cultural rights, consistent with the principles of non-discrimination and the best 
interest of families, women, and children. The UNCT will initiate and support training on the declarations 
and conventions to such groups as NGOs that work with and for women and children, teachers, social 
workers, health personnel, the judiciary, and law enforcement officials, with a view to improving access to 
justice, law enforcement, and sensitivity of both law enforcers and media. 
The UNCT will provide assistance in drafting new laws or amending existing discriminatory laws. It will 
support the formulation of Acts dealing with domestic/family violence, and provide support to the 
establishment of an independent mechanism to monitor the realization of the rights of women and children 
and to deal with individual complaints relating thereto. The UNCT will spearhead the preparation of a 
comprehensive "Bill for Children" that will seek to harmonize all legislation in relation to children with a view 
to ensuring that every child is recognized as a person and enjoys full rights. Work will continue too on a 
family code. Generally, the UNCT will continue its advocacy for full participation of children in cultural, civil, 
and political life. 
Building on its experience, the UNCT will support national initiatives to broaden the reach and impact of the 
National Insurance Scheme and to formulate social security policy and laws that take cognizance of those 
most discriminated against, including senior citizens, children, and persons living with HIV/AIDS. 
With regards to drug abuse and drug addiction, UNDCP is financing a three year project (1999-2001)in 
Guyana that is intended to strengthen the State's capacity to deal effectively with an emerging drug abuse 
caseload. The project targets both the institutional response capacity and the capacity of communities to 
cope with drug abuse and began with a study on drug abuse in the major cities. This study will provide a 
baseline reading of progress and impact throughout the duration of the project. The role of the UNCT in the 
implementation of the project is important as it allows for building on complementarity and building drug 
abuse prevention considerations into the mandates of the UNCT agencies. 12
Regardless of the efforts of the project, much more work needs to be done to achieve maximum functioning 
of the regulatory bodies that manage Guyana’s drug control strategy. Some positive advances have been 
made to counter narcotics trafficking in Guyana and new legislation is in place. However the coordinating 
role of the National Anti-Narcotic Commission (NANCOM) is not functioning effectively and needs to be 
strengthened in order to determine policy and ensure proper co-ordination of programmes as outlined in the 
National Drug Control Master Plan. Through the collaborative framework of the UNCT attention will be 
given to: 
 Building the effectiveness of the NANCOM through assistance in developing appropriate 
mechanisms of co-ordination and data collection. 
 Developing mechanisms for drug demand reduction through the strengthening of 
partnerships and networks between communities, government, non-governmental, and 
donor agencies. 
Guyana has benefited from UNDCP assistance also through regional projects. In the demand reduction 
field, Guyana has participated in a UNICEF-executed project that strives to integrate drug abuse prevention 
related contents through the Health and Family Life Education (HFLE) curriculum. Teachers in Guyana 
have participated in training sessions intended to impart a methodology, which caters to today’s classroom 
environment. 
UNDCP has actively supported Guyana in the field of forensic science through a regional project, which 
provides both equipment and training over the period 1998-2001. The Guyana Customs and Excise 
Department has also received hands on training through a UNDCP regional precursor control project 
executed by the Caribbean Customs Law Enforcement Council (CCLEC) which has trained 25 Customs 
officer in precursor chemical detection in consignments, risk profiling and targeting techniques. 
Guyana has received a Joint Mission from the Caribbean drug control Coordination Mechanism (CCM)3
and the CARICOM Drug Control Coordinator. This Mission gauged the level of progress the country has 
made in meeting the objectives of the Barbados Plan of Action. The Mission will also develop a country 
profile that makes concise recommendations to the Government of Guyana regarding the strengths and 
weakness of the national drug control efforts. 
Another priority area is that of improving data collection and dissemination. The UNCT will support the 
development of standardized, gender-disaggregated databases supported by appropriate and adequate 
research. It will, for example, access technical assistance through the UN Statistical Office to support the 
mainstreaming of gender in socioeconomic statistics and the production of gender budgets. It merits 
mention that currently the UNCT is facilitating the training of mid-level managers in population and 
development strategies at the University of the West Indies (UWI). 
(ii) Promote a) rights-awareness and access, b) meaningful participation of 
beneficiaries and other agents of change in the areas of sexual and reproductive
